interactive_questions.title: Case 1: Benford's Law Distribution Audits
interactive_questions.prompt: Observe the first-digit frequencies calculated across all quarter journal ledger records.
interactive_questions.question: Under Benford's Law, which pattern suggests potential fabricated transactions or human tampering?
options: A. Leading digits following a clean logarithmic decay curve peaking at 1.
B. A sudden, highly abnormal spike in the frequency of specific leading digits (e.g. digit 4).
C. Leading digits having completely uniform frequencies across all transactions.
interactive_questions.answer: B. A sudden, highly abnormal spike in the frequency of specific leading digits (e.g. digit 4).
interactive_questions.explanation: Human-fabricated receipts or fraud entries often over-use specific digits (e.g., $4,500), causing measurable spikes that deviate from Benford's natural log curve.

theory.title: Benford's Law in Fraud Audits
theory.content: Benford's Law dictates that in naturally occurring numerical data, the digit 1 appears as the leading significant digit ~30% of the time, decaying logarithmically to 9 (~4.6%). Abnormal deviations suggest human manipulation.
theory.analogy: A natural forest has trees of random heights, but a fake plastic forest has identical tree measurements.
theory.application: Run continuous statistical anomaly scans on journal ledgers using Chi-Square tests to isolate abnormal digit frequencies.

interactive_questions.title: Case 2: Semantic Hallucinations & Sum Reconciliation
interactive_questions.prompt: Observe an LLM agent attempting to reconcile transactions by summing up string values inside text receipts.
interactive_questions.question: What is the primary risk of relying entirely on standard LLM token generation for summing financial balances?
options: A. The LLM might round floating decimal numbers or introduce slight text-prediction addition errors.
B. The LLM will run out of context tokens and forget the balance sheets.
C. The LLM will convert dollars into foreign currencies automatically.
interactive_questions.answer: A. The LLM might round floating decimal numbers or introduce slight text-prediction addition errors.
interactive_questions.explanation: LLM text prediction is probabilistic and poor at precise float math. Accounting agents must trigger deterministic tools (like Python execution) for mathematical operations.

theory.title: Precise Financial Reconciliation
theory.content: LLMs are text generators, not algebraic calculators. To guarantee bookkeeper compliance, agents must utilize tool-use calls (Function Calling) to calculate exact decimal metrics.
theory.analogy: Asking a poet to calculate tax returns instead of using an spreadsheet application.
theory.application: Structure agent workflows to parse transaction balances into floats, and sum them using Decimal libraries in a separate runtime.

interactive_questions.title: Case 1: AI vs. Verified Tax Rules
interactive_questions.prompt: An agent is analyzing an invoice for a software subscription sold in California. The agent needs to determine the applicable sales tax rate.
interactive_questions.question: What is the most secure architecture for an AI agent to determine the correct tax rate?
options: A. Ask the LLM to predict the California sales tax based on its pre-trained knowledge base.
B. Have the agent parse the location data and query a deterministic tax rate API.
C. Prompt the LLM to search the web for 'Current California software tax rate' and extract the percentage.
interactive_questions.answer: B. Have the agent parse the location data and query a deterministic tax rate API.
interactive_questions.explanation: LLMs hallucinate and their pre-trained data can be outdated. The AI should only be used to extract the necessary parameters (location, product type) to query a deterministic, regularly updated tax API.

theory.title: Deterministic Rulesets in Tax AI
theory.content: Tax liabilities demand precision. AI agents shouldn't calculate taxes internally. Instead, they should act as orchestrators: extracting structured data from unstructured invoices, and passing that data to determinisitic, rule-based tax engines via function calling.
theory.analogy: The AI is the mailroom clerk sorting the package based on address, but the actual calculation is done by the automated postage scale.
theory.application: Use function calling / tool use to bridge the gap between unstructured document understanding and structured tax APIs.

interactive_questions.title: Case 1: Multimodal Expense Auditing
interactive_questions.prompt: An employee uploads a photo of a dinner receipt from a business trip. The receipt includes a $45 steak and a $15 alcoholic beverage.
interactive_questions.question: How should the AI agent handle this expense claim if the company policy explicitly denies reimbursement for alcohol?
options: A. Reject the entire receipt automatically and notify the employee.
B. Approve the receipt since it's a single restaurant bill and the total is under $100.
C. Extract line items, flag the alcohol, automatically deduct $15, and approve the remaining $45.
interactive_questions.answer: C. Extract line items, flag the alcohol, automatically deduct $15, and approve the remaining $45.
interactive_questions.explanation: Modern AI expense agents don't just look at the total amount. They use vision models to extract line items, map them against company policies, and perform automated deductions for non-compliant items, reducing manual HR review.

theory.title: Policy Engine Integration
theory.content: Expense AI operates as a semantic filter. It translates the visual data of a receipt into a structured JSON array of line items, then runs those items through a deterministic policy engine (e.g., 'If category == alcohol, reject').
theory.analogy: It's like a bouncer at a club checking IDs individually, rather than just looking at the group as a whole.
theory.application: Implement multimodal LLMs (like GPT-4V or Gemini Pro Vision) to parse receipts into structured schemas, followed by deterministic validation logic.
